verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “I’ve been having diarrhea for like, let’s say, past three days” as the main reason for the visit.

Duration: “been having diarrhea for like… past three days”; frequency: “around five to six times a day”; character: “it’s definitely watery. Loose stools?”; blood: “Any blood in your stools?” – “No, not that I could see.”
Onset with vomiting: “it started with vomiting, so I vomited a couple of times, but then that went away. And, yeah, it’s just diarrhea now.”
Reduced appetite/PO intake: “Have you managed to eat anything? Solids?” – “Not much… just a little bit, but I don’t really feel like I have appetite.”
Dehydration and weakness: “I feel like I can’t really drink too much… I feel very dehydrated” and later “I feel very weak, though.”
Fever early but now fine: “Probably at the beginning I was feeling… I had a bit of temperature, but now I feel… I feel kind of fine.”
Abdominal pain: “Any other symptoms, like tummy pain?” – “Not. Not really, no”; headaches/myalgias: “Any headaches or muscle pains?” – “Not really.”

Spontaneous onset at home with no triggers: “I was at home. I was working on my Computer… then I had some diarrhea straight after that”; no food trigger: “Did you have any takeaway food or any dodgy restaurant food?” – “Not that I remember”; no sick contacts: “Have you been around anyone unwell with diarrhea…?” – “Not that I know.”
Past history: “So I do suffer of asthma.”
Medication: “so I do have my [inhalers] that I… use infrequently” and clarified as “Is that a blue inhaler?” – “Yes, it is.”
Allergies: “Do you have any allergies to any medications?” – “Not that I know of.”
Family history: “My father has high… well, used to have high blood pressure. He actually… died of bowel cancer like 10 years ago.”
Mother’s history: “my mother… she has diabetes.”; when asked “Do we know if that’s type one or type two?” – “It’s type two.”
Living situation: “Oh, I live alone.”; occupation: “What do you do for work?” – “I’m a software engineer.”
Time off work: “Have you taken time off work recently?” – “Yes, yes, I have. These last three days I’ve been feeling really unwell, so I couldn’t work.”
Alcohol: “Do you do either of those [smoking and alcohol]?” – “Not really. I drink infrequently, like socially, let’s say.”
Smoking: “and I don’t smoke.”

Doctor’s assessment: “I think you’re probably suffering from what we call gastroenteritis… Normally lasts for about three to five days and gets better.” This aligns with 3 days of watery diarrhea and initial vomiting that resolved.

Patient reports feeling dehydrated with reduced intake and ongoing diarrhea: “I feel very dehydrated… I don’t really feel like I have appetite… around five to six times a day,” supporting dehydration due to decreased intake and stool losses.
Asthma control: “I do suffer of asthma… I do have my [inhalers] that I… use infrequently… Is that a blue inhaler?… Yes, it is,” supporting intermittent asthma managed with a blue inhaler as needed.
Supportive care and fluids: “The things you can do to really help yourself get better soon, you can drink plenty of fluids, really try and flush the toxins out your body.”
ORS with Diurelite: “You can get things from the pharmacy, which called Diurelite, which can help replenish any minerals and vitamins you may have lost… It’s a type of fluid replacement drink.”
Paracetamol: “You can take some paracetamol if you’re feeling feverish and weak.”
Time off work: “Would probably advise you to continue taking time off work for next day or two until you get better.”
Return criteria: “Normally you have to be diarrhea free for about 24 to 48 hours before you return back to work.”
Fluids for dehydration: “you can drink plenty of fluids, really try and flush the toxins out your body,” which is specifically aimed at supporting recovery and countering fluid loss.
Electrolyte replacement: “You can get things from the pharmacy, which called Diurelite, which can help replenish any minerals and vitamins you may have lost… It’s a type of fluid replacement drink.”
Follow-up timing: “Let’s see how the next few days go. And if you’re still not better next week, I want you to come back and see me.”
Re-contact if not improving: Patient repeats plan—“If it doesn’t, I’ll call back”—and doctor affirms, indicating instruction to re-contact if symptoms persist or do not improve.
